spoken: To make a 1944 film about the war in Tunisia, scenes were re-staged, some as far away as Florida and California.
A 1970 Hollywood film moved a Tunisian battle to Spain, and gave it the wrong German general.
And two films made in 2008 brought the war back to a villa and a courtyard in Tunis.
Four films, four ways of telling the same six months. Each shows us the war, and the time it was made.
In 1942, Tunisia was a French protectorate, ruled in name by the Bey of Tunis.
In November, German and Italian troops poured into Tunis, and Allied armies closed in from Algeria and Libya.
The fighting lasted until the 13th of May, 1943.
Tunisians of every faith, Muslims, Jews and Christians, lived through the occupation, the bombing and the battles.
Film-makers have told this story ever since. We follow four films, in the order they were made.
For each, we ask who made it and for whom, what it shows, what it invents, and what it says about its time.
Our first film was made during the war, by the armies that fought it.
British army film-makers had a hit with Desert Victory, about El Allamain, and began a film on Tunisia, Africa Freed.
Then the British and American information offices agreed on one joint film instead, Tunisian Victory.
Hollywood director Frank Capra, then a US Army colonel, made it with Britain's Hugh Stewart and some 300 staff.
It follows the campaign from the landings to the surrender. Every voice in it is British or American.
Britain's Imperial War Museum notes that it gives the American effort far more weight than Africa Freed had.
Much of it was filmed in the campaign, but much American footage was lost when German forces sank the ship carrying it.
So scenes were re-created. George Stevens, based in Algiers, spent two weeks filming tanks and troops.
John Huston filmed planes and dummy tanks in Florida and California. Whether those scenes were used is unclear.
And its two soldier narrators, one British, one American, are invented, and voiced by actors.
The two teams argued for months over who would tell it. Capra took control, and the film opened in March 1944.
Its narrators call the campaign the greatest of combined operations, and its soldiers end by hoping to build a better world together.
Made for audiences at home while the war went on, it is the armies' story.
Twenty-six years later, Hollywood came back to the battle, with Patton, made by Twentieth Century Fox.
Franklin J. Schaffner directed it from a script by Francis Ford Coppola and Edmund H. North, with George C. Scott as Patton.
In the film, after the American defeat at Kasserine, Patton takes over the shaken Second Corps.
One morning his aides wake him, because Rommel is about to attack. By the bed lies a book by Rommel on tank warfare.
As the German tanks fall back at El Guettar, Scott's Patton cries out to Rommel, I read your book!
The record is different. Rommel never finished such a book, and he had left Africa for good on 9 March 1943.
On 23 March, the German 10th Panzer Division attacked the US 1st Infantry Division in the El Guettar valley.
A minefield stopped eight tanks, American guns knocked out about 30 more, and by midday the Germans had pulled back.
The fighting went on into April. The film turns weeks into one morning, and two divisions into a duel between two generals.
Its Tunisia is not Tunisia either. Those scenes were filmed in Almeria, in the south of Spain.
Patton opened in 1970, while the United States was fighting in Vietnam.
Some saw a hero in it, others a warning. President Nixon watched it again and again.
It won seven Oscars, including Best Picture. It is one general's story, and Tunisia is only its setting.
Our third film was made by a Tunisian. Fe-reed Boogadeer was born in Hammam Lif, near Tunis, in 1944.
A historian of African and Arab cinema, he had filmed Muslim, Jewish and Christian neighbours in A Summer in La Goulette, in 1996.
In 2008 he made Villa Jasmin for French television, from a 2003 novel by the journalist Serge Mo-ah-tee.
Mo-ah-tee, born in Tunis in 1946, wrote it about his father, also named Serge, a Jewish socialist journalist.
In the film, a son comes back to Tunis in 1976 to find his parents' past.
Some of it is history. Vichy's anti-Jewish laws reached Tunisia in 1940, and German troops held Tunis from November 1942.
About 5,000 Jewish men were sent to forced labour, says the US Holocaust Memorial Museum.
Some is family memory. His daughter, Neen, recalled that he was deported to Sachsenhausen, a camp near Berlin.
She remembered a German taking Mo-ah-tee for an Italian name, and an escape helped, apparently, by a dentist.
But she could not fix the dates. The film makes its own choices, and even renames the family Boccara.
The real Serge Mo-ah-tee died in 1957. His son Henry, aged eleven, left for Paris, and later took his father's name.
Made by two men born in and near Tunis in the 1940s, it is a son's story, told from memory.
Our last film, The Wedding Song, was written and directed by the French film-maker Karin Albou.
A French-Tunisian film, mostly in Arabic and French, it opened in France in December 2008.
Tunis, 1942. Nuhr, a Muslim girl, and Miriam, a Jewish girl, are sixteen, neighbours and best friends.
Nuhr's fiancé, Khalid, works for the Germans, and forbids her to see Miriam.
The front is far away. The war reaches the girls as orders, leaflets and bombs, in their own street.
The girls are invented, like Khalid, and Raoul, the rich older doctor Miriam must marry. The orders are history.
On 6 December 1942, the Germans demanded Jewish workers in Tunis, and about 4,000 men were sent to forced labour.
On 22 December, they levied 20 million francs on the Jewish community. A US report of June 1943 records both.
In the film, Miriam's mother marries her off because money is needed for that levy, and Raoul ends up in forced labour.
German leaflets in the film court the Muslims and blame the Jews, as Nazi radio did in Arabic.
Made more than sixty years later, it puts a friendship between a Muslim and a Jewish girl at the heart of the war.
In December 2017, it was shown in Tunis to mark 75 years since the roundup of 9 December 1942.
Put the four films side by side, and you can watch the story change hands.
In 1944, the armies told their own victory, in British and American voices, while the war went on.
In 1970, Hollywood told one American general's story, and Spain stood in for Tunisia.
In 2008, a Tunisian director and a French-Tunisian film turned to the people of Tunis, Jewish and Muslim.
The camera moved from the front line to a villa and a courtyard, and from generals to neighbours.
So every war film is a source twice over, about the war, and about its own time.
The fighting lasted six months; its films span more than sixty years. Watch them, and ask who is telling.
